title: The conversation cannot wait
summary: OpenAI's GPT-Live engineering post reveals the fast media path, prepared state handoffs, asynchronous reasoning, and shadow testing behind continuous voice. Then OpenAI's response in Apple's trade-secret case exposes a messier systems problem: offboarding controls that failed to make access and permission legible.

threads.name: Apple v. OpenAI trade-secret suit
threads.status: OpenAI published its August 3 response to Apple's preliminary-injunction request, including redacted messages showing Apple employees asking former engineer Chang Liu for technical help after his departure and correspondence documenting a misdirected message from Apple's outside counsel; the court has not resolved the dispute.
threads.arc: The case moves from Apple's broad theft allegations to a contested documentary record in which the same post-departure exchanges can be framed as unauthorized access or Apple-sanctioned transition help.

dives.story: GPT-Live's production architecture for continuous voice
dives.why_it_matters: Teams building realtime voice agents need to engineer around frame deadlines, long-lived state, tool latency, and whole-system concurrency; faster model inference alone does not keep a conversation live.

dives.story: OpenAI's documentary response in the Apple trade-secret case
dives.why_it_matters: Organizations hiring from competitors need auditable offboarding and transition channels, because residual access plus informal requests from former colleagues can make the boundary between authorized continuity and alleged misuse impossible to reconstruct cleanly.

concepts_taught: real-time fast-path architecture: isolate deadline-bound media from asynchronous tools and reasoning, prepare replacement state beside the live session, and measure capacity in concurrent sessions that keep every frame on schedule
